summary: Extends the Alternate-Marking method of RFC 8321, which measures packet loss and delay in a network by marking packets, from point-to-point flows to flows that can follow several paths, a multipoint-to-multipoint setting. It is experimental and was later replaced by RFC 9342.

eli5.summary: To check how well a network delivers, you can paint packets in alternating colors and count them at two spots. This document extends that trick to flows that split and merge along many paths. It was replaced by RFC 9342.

how does network clustering help measurement

subtitle: Measuring packet loss and delay across paths that split and merge in the network

tldr.problem: The Alternate-Marking method (RFC 8321) measures packet loss and delay, but only for simple point-to-point paths. In modern networks, traffic often splits across multiple paths (load balancing) or merges from multiple sources, and the original method does not work for these multipath scenarios.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends Alternate-Marking to handle multipoint flows by partitioning the network into clusters—smallest subnetworks where packets flowing in equals packets flowing out. By measuring traffic at each cluster boundary, operators can locate problems without tracking every individual packet.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can measure loss and delay across complex multipath topologies and progressively zoom into problematic areas. It was replaced by RFC 9342.

today: RFC 8889 is an Experimental specification and has been replaced by RFC 9342. The technique of using Alternate-Marking with network clustering remains valuable for operators managing complex multipath networks, SD-WAN, and large-scale infrastructure who need flexible, scalable performance monitoring without the overhead of point-to-point measurement of every flow combination.

sections.title: Extending Alternate-Marking to Multipath Networks
sections.content:
Alternate-Marking, defined in RFC 8321, is a passive measurement technique that divides a packet flow into batches marked with alternating colors (batches A and B, alternating at each marking period). By counting colored packets at two measurement points, operators can calculate packet loss and delay without sending test traffic.

But Alternate-Marking assumes all packets flow through the same two measurement points in a simple point-to-point path. In real networks, packets take multiple paths due to load balancing, multipath routing (ECMP), or when monitoring aggregate flows. This RFC extends the method to handle any flow whose packets can follow different paths—from point-to-multipoint, multipoint-to-point, or full multipoint-to-multipoint topologies.
sections.eli5: The old method colors packets and counts them at two spots. The new method works even when packets split up and take many different roads through the network.

sections.title: Flow Definition and Clustering
sections.content:
The key insight is that packets in a multipath flow can be identified by flexible rules—not just the traditional 5-tuple (source IP, destination IP, protocol, source port, destination port). For example, you could select all packets from one source address, or all packets to one destination, creating flows that naturally split or merge across multiple paths.

Instead of tracking individual packets, the method partitions the monitored network into clusters—smallest identifiable subnetworks where the number of packets entering equals the number exiting. Within a cluster, packet loss can be detected, but not localized to a specific link. By applying the packet loss equation at each cluster, operators can identify which cluster contains the problem and drill down progressively.

A cluster algorithm groups network links by shared starting nodes, then joins them if they share ending nodes. This produces a minimal set of clusters that partition the monitored path.
sections.eli5: Instead of tracking each packet, you count packets at cluster boundaries. If more packets go in than come out, something is lost in that cluster.

sections.title: Measuring Loss and Delay Across Clusters
sections.content:
For packet loss, the formula is simple: Loss = (sum of packets at all input nodes) minus (sum of packets at all output nodes). This total loss can be computed for the entire monitored network, or independently for each cluster.

For delay and delay variation, the RFC offers two approaches. First, delay can be measured as the difference between mean timestamps at input and output nodes, weighted by packet counts (useful for cluster-level measurements). Second, for single-packet measurements in multipath scenarios, the method uses dynamic hashing—selecting a sample of packets by hash value, then matching their timestamps at input and output boundaries to compute per-packet delay across any path.

The dynamic hashing approach adapts the hash function to maintain a target sample size even when packet rates vary, preventing measurement overflow while preserving statistical properties across different paths.
sections.eli5: Count packets going in and out of each cluster to find loss. For delay, compare arrival timestamps at entry and exit points.

sections.title: Timing Alignment and Network Zooming
sections.content:
When multiple source nodes mark packets independently, their marking clocks may not be synchronized. The RFC addresses this by requiring that the available counting interval (the time window where measurements are reliable) must exceed the clock misalignment between sources plus the network delay. This constraint ensures that packet batches from different sources do not contaminate measurements at exit points.

The RFC describes a network zooming approach: start by measuring the entire monitored network or broad clusters. If a problem is detected (too much loss or delay), the operator reconfigures filters to split clusters further or activates additional measurement points, progressively narrowing down the problematic area. This hierarchical approach reduces the overhead of continuous detailed monitoring while enabling quick diagnosis when needed.

This method fits well with Software-Defined Networking (SDN), where a central controller can orchestrate which flows and clusters to monitor based on current network conditions and detected problems.
sections.eli5: Clocks on different routers might not be perfect, so you need enough time between color changes to avoid mixing up packets. When you find a problem, zoom in on that cluster for more detail.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
The RFC lists several deployment scenarios:

  • VPNs: Monitor aggregate traffic from all customers to one endpoint, reducing the number of flows and measurement points compared to point-to-point monitoring.
  • Mobile Backhaul: Track traffic by source or destination EnodeB address, resulting in one monitored flow per cell site instead of per customer connection.
  • Over-the-Top Services: Monitor traffic from all OTT servers as one multipoint flow in each direction, reducing complexity in large-scale content delivery.
  • Enterprise SD-WAN: Measure per-cluster and per-flow performance to inform path selection and policy enforcement across WAN links.

Unlike RFC 8321, which applies only to point-to-point unicast and broadcast traffic, Multipoint Alternate Marking handles anycast and Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) flows. The method is agnostic to how counters and timestamps are transported, leaving implementation choices open.
sections.eli5: This technique helps network operators monitor everything from cellular networks to cloud services to wide-area networks, reducing the work needed to track all the paths traffic takes.
